messages.subject: [statnet_help] comparing parameter estimates across models
messages.body_plain:
Greetings.
I have data with one set of nodes and two sets of edges
(friendship and academic ties among the same set of subjs).

I am using two instances of the same ergm (except for the DV)
to predict the two edge-sets.

I'd like to statistically compare the parameter estimates
across the two models (e.g., is racial homophily significantly
stronger for friendship vs. academic ties?).

The Chow test adapted to logistic regression requires pooling
data, and I've been thinking about trying this using the union
of the two edgesets and edge-covariate dummies to indicate the
source edgeset, or pooling and adding an interaction term, but
this is somewhat beyond my depth.

Any suggestions?

Thanks
Brian

-- 
Brian Rubineau
Assistant Professor, Organizational Behavior          146K Ives Hall
School of Industrial and Labor Relations            ph. 607.255.3048
Cornell University                                 fax. 810.963.2738
Ithaca, NY 14850                               brubineau@cornell.edu

simulation when using the new specifications:

>model.02.1 <- ergm(g~edges + gwdegree)

edges  -6.9715754 1.764e-01  <1e-04  3.081e-02

messages.subject: [statnet_help] How to asses convergence a possible bug
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] How to asses convergence a possible bug
messages.body_plain:
> Can anyone give me quick pointers on how to asses it the convergence of the 
> ergm model is good. I have used the function mcmc.diagnostics, but am not

Hello Ales,

A great question.  It turns out that we (the statnet development team) are 
in the process of putting together a special journal issue on statnet, and 
there will be some more guidance in there on assessing model convergence 
(as well as many other topics - stay tuned!)

My own personal set of heuristics for considering model convergence is as 
follows:

(1) Using the verbose=T argument in ergm, check to see whether the density 
of the returned network is roughly the same as the density of the initial 
network for each iteration of the fitting algorithm.  If the network is 
heading towards an empty or full network, this will be a sure sign of 
problems.  Of course if you are using an MCMC proposal that fixes density, 
this is not an option.

(2) Check the MCMC diagnostic plots.  The plots on the left should have no 
sustained trend away from their original value.  There will certainly 
be short-term trends (such is the nature of MCMC) but in the long-term it 
should vary around the oringial value.  The plots on the right should be 
centered around the original value, and will generally be unimodal if all 
is well.

(3) Check the log-likelihood ratio that is printed out with each iteration 
of the fitting algorithm.  A small value (often less than 1) is good.  If 
it starts creeping up towards 20 (which is where the software caps 
estimating it) then there is likely to be a problem.

(4) Within the verbose output, look for the summary of the simluation.  In 
the later iterations, the values for "mean" should be close to zero, and 
the std. t units should also be low, or at least declining with successive 
iterations.  This tells you how far away your simulated statistics are 
from your observed statistics.

Generally I find that the results from these different measures have a 
high degree of concordance - if one shows a problem, they all do.  So one 
doesn't necessarily have to check all, but collectively they can give you 
a very good sense whether your model convergence is good or not.

> Are there any other options. Are there any suggestions what can be done 
> besides selecting better starting values, increasing MCMC sample size and 
> selecting terms that are not correlated?

I am a big fan of using TNT for the proposal type instead of 
constantedges.  That plus a large MCMC sample size, should help in most 
cases where the model is a good one.  The new version of statnet to be 
released soon will have additional aids to convergence as well.

> Somethimes, when I run "mcmc.diagnostics", I get "NaN" for some terms in the 
> correlations and the convergence statistics is missing for these terms. These 
> are the same terms that have NA for MCMC s.e. in summary output.  What does 
> this mean.

Could you send an example?

> Aslo, when I sepcify theta0 (starting values that are therefore not estimated 
> using maximum pseudo-likelihood ), I get the following error when I run the 
> summary on ergm object:
> "Error in -object$mplefit$hessian : invalid argument to unary operator"
> Probably because the ergm object does not have the element "mplefit".

Thanks for letting us know - we'll look into it and fix any bugs.

Cheers,
Steve

>
>
> Best regarads,
> Ales Ziberna
>
> _______________________________________________
> statnet_help mailing list
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> https://mailman1.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help

messages.subject: [statnet_help] User input for improving statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

As you may have gleaned from a number of previous emails, the statnet 
development team is planning two major releases in the coming months. The first 
is a special issue of the Journal of Statistical Software devoted to statnet. 
The second is a major new release of statnet, with various new features, bug 
fixes, and improved user interface.  These two events will be timed to coincide 
as closely as possible.

We're writing to request any knowledge you may have of existing bugs in 
statnet.  Even if there's something that you're not sure is a bug, but which 
you think may be, let us know.  Information on any documentation errors you've 
encountered would be great too (although we've fixed quite a few of these 
already).

In addition, if you have other ideas about user interface, let us know 
those too.  We can't guarantee we can implement all of these, but we will 
certainly make an effort to address those that are easy to change and/or 
seem to be common concerns.

We've been working hard to incorporate new functionality based on our own 
research needs and some user feedback.  At this point, we're not likely to be 
able to incorporate much additional user-suggested functionality, but if 
there's something that you feel would strongly enhance statnet and would be

me instead of the whole statnet listserv.

Cheers all,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] statnet source code
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  Recently I've seen a few requests for the source code for  
statnet and since I haven't seen a response, I thought I'd let  
everyone know how to get it.  In a word, wait. :)  Currently we on  
the development team are knee-deep in a major reorganization of the  
code in preparation for releasing on CRAN (the Comprehensive R  
Archive Network -- see www.r-project.org) a package called "ergm"  
which, together with the "network" package and others that are  
already on CRAN, will comprise all of the current functionality of  
statnet.  In case you're wondering, "statnet" will still exist, but  
it will technically be just a wrapper for the "network" and "ergm"  
packages.

So, at the moment we don't have any code to share because we're still  
busy reorganizing it.  But once we're through this process, which  
should culminate sometime in late December, we'll have a much more --  
we hope -- readable version of the code for those who are  
interested.  Also, truth be told, even if we had something to  
release, we'd need to wait until we get all of the license details in  
place (a slightly modified GPL v.3 with attribution), which appears  
to be almost done.  The bottom line on that is, please cite us if you  
use this code and be explicit if you reuse it in other code -- but  
you already knew that!

We'll DEFINITELY let you know when the package is released on CRAN.   
Thanks for your patience.

Dave

PS.  There will also be a series of papers coming out in the Journal  
of Statistical Software (jstatsoft.org) that we hope will serve as a  
fairly comprehensive manual for all the statnet-related software.   
Many of you will already know much of this material, but we hope that  
these articles will be handy references.  Publication will coincide  
with the CRAN release.




David Hunter
Associate professor
Department of Statistics
Penn State University
Phone:  (814) 863-0979
Fax:  (814) 863-7114
www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter
